mcqs.question: An image with large areas of solid color is encrypted with AES in ECB mode. What happens to the image's structure?
options: The image becomes fully random noise with no visible structure
The structure is preserved in the ciphertext, because identical plaintext blocks always encrypt to identical ciphertext blocks under ECB
ECB refuses to encrypt image data at all
The structure is preserved only if the key is shorter than 128 bits
mcqs.explanation: ECB encrypts each block independently with no chaining, so identical input blocks — like a repeated solid-color region — always produce identical output blocks, letting the shape leak straight through the encryption. This is the exact effect the "ECB penguin" demonstration makes visible.

mcqs.question: In the ECB penguin demonstration, the same image encrypted with CBC mode looks like pure random noise, while the ECB version still shows the penguin's outline. What does this prove?
options: CBC uses a stronger key than ECB by default
That the choice of mode, not the underlying cipher, determines whether structure in the plaintext leaks into the ciphertext
That AES itself is broken when used in ECB mode
That image files cannot be encrypted correctly by any block cipher
mcqs.explanation: Both images use the identical cipher (AES) and key — the only difference is the mode of operation. CBC's chaining makes each block's ciphertext depend on everything before it, eliminating the repeated-block leak that ECB's independence allows, which is exactly the point the demonstration is making.

mcqs.question: A web service decrypts a CBC-encrypted cookie and returns a distinctly different error message when the padding is invalid versus when it's valid. Why is this dangerous?
options: It has no security impact, since padding errors are purely cosmetic
It only affects performance, not confidentiality
It leaks one bit of information per request that an attacker can exploit, repeated thousands of times, to decrypt the entire ciphertext without ever learning the key — a padding-oracle attack
It means the service is using ECB mode instead of CBC
mcqs.explanation: A padding-oracle attack uses exactly this kind of distinguishable feedback — even an error message or timing difference — as a one-bit-per-query oracle, and with enough queries an attacker can decrypt an entire CBC ciphertext without the key. This is precisely why unauthenticated CBC is considered risky and authenticated modes like GCM are preferred.

mcqs.question: Why is AES-256-GCM generally preferred over 'AES-256-CBC plus a separately computed HMAC' for new systems, even though both can provide confidentiality and integrity?
options: GCM combines encryption and authentication into one construction and one pass, removing the risk of getting the encrypt-then-MAC ordering or implementation wrong, which has historically been a real source of vulnerabilities
CBC mode cannot be combined with HMAC under any circumstances
GCM does not require a nonce, unlike CBC's IV
HMAC is cryptographically weaker than GCM's authentication mechanism
mcqs.explanation: GCM is a single authenticated-encryption construction, so there's no separate ordering decision (encrypt-then-MAC vs MAC-then-encrypt) to get right or wrong — a decision that has caused real vulnerabilities when implemented incorrectly by hand. GCM still needs a nonce, just like CTR, since it's built on the same counter-mode foundation.

mcqs.question: According to the comparison of ECB, CBC, CTR, and GCM, which single property does only GCM provide among the four?
options: The ability to encrypt data of any length
Resistance to nonce reuse under all conditions
Parallelizable encryption across blocks
Built-in integrity/authentication alongside confidentiality, with no separate MAC step required
mcqs.explanation: ECB, CBC, and CTR all provide confidentiality alone (with CBC and CTR avoiding ECB's structural leak) but none of them authenticate the data on their own — GCM is the only one of the four with integrity built into the same construction. Parallelizability is shared with CTR, and none of the four is safe under nonce reuse.

mcqs.question: A service reuses the same nonce with the same AES-GCM key across two different messages due to a bug. What is the concrete consequence?
options: Only a minor performance degradation occurs, with no security impact
The two ciphertexts get XORed with the same keystream, which can be exploited to recover both plaintexts, and GCM's authentication guarantee is also broken, potentially allowing forged tags
The messages simply fail to decrypt and are discarded safely
AES automatically detects the reuse and generates a new nonce internally
mcqs.explanation: Nonce reuse under GCM (built on CTR) means the same keystream segment encrypts two different messages — XORing the ciphertexts cancels the keystream and can expose both plaintexts, and separately, nonce reuse breaks GCM's authentication tag guarantees, which is why this specific mistake is treated as catastrophic rather than a minor bug.
